steps.line: Tomorrow you speak in court, five charges to answer in order. Keep them here, not on a scroll.
Walk the colonnade from the door. At each place, set one strange picture of one charge.

steps.text: Go to the first empty place

steps.act: Set the first image: a man on fire (the arson)

steps.text: The next place

steps.act: Set the second: a goat in a toga (the forged will)

steps.text: The next place

steps.act: Set the third: a huge ear (the witness who overheard)

steps.text: The next place

steps.act: Set the fourth: a bloody knife (the assault)

steps.text: The next place, by the golden hand

steps.act: Set the fifth: a donkey in a crown (the bribe)

steps.line: Five places, five pictures. The stranger they are, the longer they stay.

steps.text: Go to the court in the Forum, and stand where the advocate stands

steps.line: The praetor nods. Speak. Walk your house again, from the door, and read your pictures in order.

steps.text: Walk your places again, in order

steps.act: Speak the fifth charge, and close

steps.line: Every charge answered, in order, without a scroll. Do it again tomorrow, and the next day.
On a given finite straight line, to construct an equilateral triangle. The line is AB, pegged out on the sand.

steps.text: Go to A

steps.act: Drive the peg in at A

steps.text: Go to B, paying out the cord

steps.act: Tie the cord at B: it is exactly as long as AB

steps.line: Postulate 3: a circle may be drawn with any centre and distance. Walk round A with the cord taut.

steps.text: Walk the circle round A, the cord taut

steps.line: Every point you walked is as far from A as B is. Now round B, through A.

steps.text: Walk the circle round B, the cord taut

steps.line: The two circles cross. Where they cross is the third corner.

steps.text: Stand where the circles cross

steps.act: Drive in the peg at C, and stretch the cord to A and to B

steps.line: CA equals AB, for both reach from A to its circle. CB equals BA, from B to its circle.
Things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another. So CA equals CB, and all three are equal.
Being what it was required to do.
A right-angled triangle with sides of three, four and five, and a square of tiles on each side.

steps.text: Step on every tile of the square on the short side

steps.line: Nine.

steps.text: Now every tile of the square on the other short side

steps.line: Sixteen. Nine and sixteen make twenty-five.

steps.text: Now every tile of the square on the long side, opposite the right angle

steps.line: Twenty-five. The square on the side opposite the right angle equals the squares on the other two.
Counting shows it for this triangle. Euclid's proof shows it for every right-angled triangle there is.
Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans.
Agamemnon takes your prize, the girl Briseis, before the whole army. You are in two minds: kill him, or check your anger.
Minerva came down from heaven and seized the son of Peleus by his yellow hair, visible to him alone.
“Why are you here, daughter of aegis-bearing Jove? To see the pride of Agamemnon, son of Atreus?”

steps.act: Put the sword back in its sheath

steps.line: You obey the goddess. But you will not fight for him again, and the Achaeans will die for your anger.
At the Scaean gate Andromache runs to meet you, and the nurse behind her with your little son.
The boy is scared at the sight of his father's armour, and at the horse-hair plume that nodded fiercely from his helmet.
Hector took the helmet from his head and laid it all gleaming upon the ground.

steps.act: Take your son in your arms

steps.line: Then he took his darling child, kissed him, and dandled him in his arms.
You know Troy will fall. You will go back to the fight anyway, for the city, and for the glory men will remember.
Odysseus, old Phoenix and Ajax come to your hut. Agamemnon offers gold, horses, women, his daughter, seven cities.
“Though you hate both him and his gifts with all your heart, yet pity the rest of the Achaeans.”
“Him do I hate even as the gates of hell who says one thing while he hides another in his heart.”
Old Phoenix, who raised you, weeps and begs you not to wait until it is too late.
Ajax says it plainly: you are hard, and you care nothing for the friends who honoured you.
Three times asked, three times refused. Your honour is not for sale. Your friends go on dying.
Your mother brings the arms the fire god made you in one night. On the shield is the whole world.
He wrought the earth, the heavens, and the sea; the moon also at her full and the untiring sun.

steps.text: Walk the city at peace: a wedding, a quarrel judged by the elders
Walk the city at war, and the ambush by the river
Walk the ploughland, the harvest and the vintage
Walk the dance, and the river Ocean round the rim

steps.line: War is one ring of it. Everything else goes on round it: weddings, trials, harvests, dances.
Hector waits alone before the Scaean gate. When he sees you coming, he turns and runs.

steps.text: Run after him along the wall (Shift to run)

steps.line: So did these two run full speed three times round the city of Priam. All the gods watched them.
Jove holds up his golden scales. Hector's fate sinks down toward the house of Hades.

steps.text: On past the springs where the women washed in peacetime

steps.line: Hector stands at last. He knows he will die, and he will not die without a fight.
Hector falls. Killing him does not bring back Patroclus.
You are Priam, old king of Troy. Hermes has led you through the Greek camp by night, with a wagon of ransom.

steps.text: Go into the hut of the man who killed your son

steps.line: He clasped his knees and kissed the dread murderous hands that had slain so many of his sons.
“Fear, O Achilles, the wrath of heaven; think on your own father and have compassion upon me.”
He weeps for his father; you weep for your son. Then he gives you Hector's body to take home.
The Cyclops has shut you in his cave with a stone no team could shift, and has eaten six of your men.
He is drunk on your wine, and asks your name.
“Cyclops, you ask my name and I will tell it you ... my name is Noman.”

steps.act: Drive the stake into his eye

steps.line: He roars that Noman is killing him. The other Cyclopes decide he is mad, and go home.

steps.text: Get under the great ram

steps.line: Their master felt the backs of all the sheep, without being sharp enough to find the men under their bellies.

steps.text: Out into the daylight

steps.line: Cunning got you out. Shouting your real name back from the ship will bring the sea god's anger after you.
Twenty years gone. You come home as a beggar, and the suitors are eating your house.
Penelope sets them a contest: string the old bow and shoot through twelve axes. None of them can bend it.
He strung it as easily as a skilled bard strings a new peg of his lyre.
It sang sweetly under his touch like the twittering of a swallow.
The house is yours again. But Penelope will not believe it is you until you prove it.

steps.text: Go to the bed you built

steps.line: “There was a young olive growing within the precincts of the house ... I built my room round this.”

steps.act: Tell her the secret of the bed

steps.line: Only you could know it. She runs to you. You are home.
Circe warned you: whoever hears the Sirens and goes near them never sees home again.
“Bind me as I stand upright, with a bond so fast that I cannot possibly break away.”

steps.act: Let your men bind you to the mast

steps.line: They row on with wax in their ears. The Sirens sing that they know everything that happened at Troy.
The more you beg, the tighter they bind you. The song fades astern.
At the edge of Ocean, where the sun never shines, you dig the trench and pour the blood.
The dead come up out of Erebus in crowds, with a strange cry, wanting the blood.

steps.act: Hold your sword out over the blood

steps.line: Your mother's shade comes. You reach for her three times, and three times she slips through your arms.
The seer drinks, and tells you the way home, and what it will cost.
You are Gyges, a shepherd of the king of Lydia. There was a storm, and an earthquake opened the ground where your flock was feeding.

steps.text: Go down into the opening

steps.line: Among other marvels, “a hollow brazen horse, having doors.” Inside lies a dead body more than human, wearing only a gold ring.

steps.text: Stoop and look in at the horse's door

steps.act: Take the ring from the finger of the dead

steps.text: Climb out, and join the shepherds at their monthly meeting

steps.line: They are making their report about the flocks to the king. You sit among them, turning the ring on your finger.

steps.act: Turn the collet of the ring inward

steps.line: “Instantly he became invisible to the rest of the company and they began to speak of him as if he were no longer present.”
They see you again. Gyges went to court, seduced the queen, killed the king with her help, and took the kingdom.
Glaucon: give a just man such a ring and he will do as the unjust do. No one is just of his own free will.
Would you be? Socrates must show that justice is worth having even if no one ever sees it.
The city is just: each order doing its own work. Now turn it round. The same three are in you.
Appetite, in the belly: it wants food, drink and gain, many-headed. Bronze and iron, like the producers.
Spirit, in the chest: anger, honour, courage. Silver, like the soldiers. Well trained, it sides with reason.
Reason, in the head: it loves learning and sees the whole. Gold, like the rulers. It should rule.

steps.act: Let reason rule, with spirit its ally

steps.line: “The just man does not permit the several elements within him to interfere with one another.”
“He sets in order his own inner life, and is his own master and his own law, and at peace with himself.”
“Now take a line which has been cut into two unequal parts, and divide each of them again in the same proportion.”

steps.text: Walk into the first length: images

steps.line: “By images I mean, in the first place, shadows, and in the second place, reflections in water.”

steps.text: Walk on to the things themselves

steps.line: “The animals which we see, and everything that grows or is made”: the tree, the horse, the bowl.

steps.text: Walk on to the figures inlaid in the terrace

steps.line: Here the mind reasons from hypotheses, using drawn figures to think about the square itself, the diagonal itself.

steps.act: Trace the square and its diagonal

steps.text: Walk out onto the white terrace

steps.line: Now reason itself, with no images, climbing to a first principle that rests on nothing else.
“The sun is not only the author of visibility in all visible things, but of generation and nourishment and growth.”
So the good gives things their being and the mind its knowledge, “yet the good is not essence, but far exceeds essence.”
Four faculties: reason, understanding, faith, and the perception of shadows. Each is as clear as its objects are true.
“Behold! human beings living in a underground den, which has a mouth open towards the light.”
Shadows pass on the wall: a horse, a jar, a man, a tree. You have never seen anything else. You give them names.
“You have shown me a strange image, and they are strange prisoners.” “Like ourselves, I replied.”

steps.act: Your chains are loosed. Turn round

steps.line: A fire, and men carrying figures along a wall. What you took for the real were shadows of copies. The light hurts.

steps.text: Climb the steep and rugged way up

steps.line: “When he approaches the light his eyes will be dazzled, and he will not be able to see anything at all.”
“First he will see the shadows best, next the reflections of men and other objects in the water, and then the objects.”

steps.act: Lift your eyes to the sky

steps.line: Last of all the sun itself, which makes the seasons and governs all that you once saw below.
He would rather be “the poor servant of a poor master” than live as they live. But the others are still down there.

steps.text: Go back down into the den

steps.line: Your eyes are full of darkness. They laugh: he went up and came back blind. Education is turning the whole soul round.

er.title: The myth of Er, Republic X

steps.line: You are a soul in the meadow, a thousand years after your last life. Before you, the Fates, and the spindle of Necessity.

steps.text: Go before the prophet of Lachesis

steps.line: “Your genius will not be allotted to you, but you will choose your genius.”
“Virtue is free ... the responsibility is with the chooser—God is justified.”
The first lot comes forward and in a moment chooses the greatest tyranny. Too late he sees he must devour his children.
Odysseus has the last lot. Tired of ambition, he searches a long time for the life of a private man with no cares.

steps.text: Walk among the patterns of lives

steps.act: Choose a life, and think what it will make of your soul

steps.text: March on to the river of Unmindfulness

steps.act: Drink no more than you must

steps.line: “Those who were not saved by wisdom drank more than was necessary; and each one as he drank forgot all things.”
Er did not drink. He woke on his pyre on the twelfth day and told it: “the tale has been saved and has not perished.”
Athens, 399 BC. You are Socrates, seventy years old, before five hundred and one jurors. Meletus accuses you.

steps.text: Step up to speak

steps.line: “I am that gadfly which God has attached to the state, and all day long and in all places am always fastening upon you.”

steps.act: Tell them what you really think

steps.line: “The unexamined life is not worth living.”
They vote: guilty, by a few votes. As your penalty you propose free meals for life. They vote again: death.
“The hour of departure has arrived, and we go our ways—I to die, and you to live. Which is better God only knows.”
The evening of the last day. Your friends are round you. Crito: “the sun is still upon the hill-tops.”
Do not hurry, he says; there is time enough. But you ask for the cup to be brought.

steps.act: Take the cup from the servant of the Eleven

steps.line: “Then raising the cup to his lips, quite readily and cheerfully he drank off the poison.”

steps.text: Walk about until your legs begin to fail
Lie down on the bed

steps.line: They weep. You ask them to be quiet: a man should die in peace.
“Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?”
“Of all the men of his time whom I have known, he was the wisest and justest and best.”
Heaven hid his children in the earth. Kronos, the youngest, took the jagged sickle from their mother and cut him down.
“He learned from Earth and starry Heaven that he was destined to be overcome by his own son.” So he swallows them.
You are Rhea, his wife. Five children he has swallowed. The sixth, Zeus, you have hidden in a cave in Crete.

steps.text: Go to the stone

steps.act: Wrap the stone in swaddling clothes

steps.text: Bring it to Kronos

steps.line: “He took it in his hands and thrust it down into his belly: wretch! he knew not ... his son was left behind.”
Zeus grows up, makes Kronos vomit up his children, the stone first, and overthrows him. Sons overthrow fathers.
Zeus will not wait to be overthrown in his turn. He swallows Wisdom herself, Metis, and keeps her counsel inside him.
Prometheus “stole the far-seen gleam of unwearying fire in a hollow fennel stalk.” Now he hangs chained on his crag.
As the price of fire, Zeus had the gods make a woman, and each gave her a gift. She was called Pandora, All-gifts.
Prometheus warned his brother never to take a gift from Zeus. Epimetheus took her, and understood too late.

steps.text: Go to the great jar

steps.line: “The woman took off the great lid of the jar with her hands and scattered all these.” Sickness, toil, old age.
“Only Hope remained there in an unbreakable home within under the rim of the great jar, and did not fly out.”
“But the rest, countless plagues, wander amongst men.” Is Hope kept for us, or kept from us? Hesiod does not say.

the_year.title: The farmer's year, Works and Days

steps.line: Your brother Perses took more than his share of your father's farm, by bribing the judges. Hesiod tells him: work.
“Between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her.”
“Mark, when you hear the voice of the crane who cries year by year from the clouds above, for she give the signal for ploughing.”

steps.text: Take the plough behind the oxen

steps.line: There are no shortcuts. The man who puts off his work wrestles with ruin, and ends by begging at his neighbour's door.

steps.text: Go to the threshing floor

steps.line: “When the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, are rising, begin your harvest, and your ploughing when they are going to set.”

steps.text: Go to the hives

steps.line: The idle man is like the drones, who eat what the bees have worked for. Gods and men are angry with him.

steps.act: Put up your harvest for the winter

steps.line: “Work is no disgrace: it is idleness which is a disgrace.”
A strip of papyrus, torn, from a rubbish heap in Egypt, a thousand years after she sang. Nine books; almost nothing is left.

steps.text: Find the next strip

steps.line: “And round about the [breeze] murmurs cool through apple-boughs, and slumber streams from quivering leaves.”

steps.text: Find the next strip

steps.line: “The stars about the fair moon in their turn hide their bright face when she at about her full lights up all earth.”

steps.text: Find the next strip

steps.line: “As the sweet-apple blushes on the end of the bough ... which the gatherers overlooked, nay overlooked not but could not reach.”

steps.text: Find the next strip

steps.line: “Evening, thou that bringest all that bright morning scattered; thou bringest the sheep, the goat, the child back to her mother.”

steps.text: Find the next strip

steps.line: “The moon has set, and the Pleiades; it is midnight, the time is going by, and I sleep alone.”
The [breeze] in brackets is not hers: a scholar guessed the missing word. Every reader of Sappho fills the gaps.
A whole line here, half a line there. The rest is gone forever, and what is left is sharper for it.

steps.text: Stand before the altar

steps.line: “Immortal Aphrodite of the broidered throne, daughter of Zeus, weaver of wiles, I pray thee break not my spirit.”
“Come hither, if ever before thou didst hear my voice afar, and listen.”
“Fair fleet sparrows drew thee, flapping fast their wings around the dark earth, from heaven through mid sky.”
“Thou, blessed one, smiling with immortal countenance, didst ask What now is befallen me, and Why now I call.”
“Who wrongs thee, Sappho? For even if she flies she shall soon follow, and if she rejects gifts shall yet give.”
“Come, I pray thee, now too, and release me from cruel cares ... and be thyself my ally.”

steps.text: Sit on the seat opposite

steps.line: “That man seems to me peer of gods, who sits in thy presence, and hears close to him thy sweet speech and lovely laughter.”
“That indeed makes my heart flutter in my bosom. For when I see thee but a little, I have no utterance left.”
“My tongue is broken down, and straightway a subtle fire has run under my skin, with my eyes I have no sight.”
“My ears ring, sweat pours down, and a trembling seizes all my body; I am paler than grass.”
“And seem in my madness little better than one dead. But I must dare all ...” The rest is lost.
“I pray the gods to quit me of my toils, To close the watch I keep, this livelong year.”
A year on the palace roof, “as a watch-dog lying,” waiting for the fire that will say Troy has fallen.

steps.act: Watch the far height through the night

steps.line: “Fire of the night, that brings my spirit day, Shedding on Argos light, and dance, and song.”
Mountain to mountain the beacons have run from Troy. The king is coming home. The watchman is glad, and afraid.
“The home itself might soothliest tell its tale.” Ten years ago, at Aulis, the king killed his daughter for a wind.
You are Agamemnon, home from Troy after ten years, the captive Cassandra in your chariot.
“Sweet lord, step forth, Step from thy car, I pray—nay, not on earth Plant the proud foot, O king, that trod down Troy!”
“Women! why tarry ye, whose task it is To spread your monarch’s path with tapestry?”

steps.act: Refuse: such honour is for gods, not men

steps.line: She presses. What would Priam have done, if he had won? You are tired, and you give way.
“Stepping thus upon the sea’s rich dye, I pray, Let none among the gods look down With jealous eye on me.”

steps.text: Walk the purple into your house

steps.line: “O I am sped—a deep, a mortal blow.”
“O! O! again, another, another blow!” In the bath, caught in a robe like a net. Outside, the old men cannot agree what to do.
Athens. Orestes has killed his mother to avenge his father. The Furies have hunted him here, to Athena's city.
“Slaying her husband, she did slay my sire.” “Therefore thou livest.” The Furies will not let a mother's blood be.
Athena will not judge alone. She chooses citizens, sworn to judge by the evidence, and sets them on the hill of Ares.
“Ye who judge, Arise, take each his vote, mete out the right, Your oath revering.”

steps.text: Go down to the urns

steps.line: The votes are counted. They fall even: half for the Furies, half for Orestes.
“Mine is the right to add the final vote, And I award it to Orestes’ cause.”
The Furies rage. Athena does not drive them out: she offers them a home under the hill, and honour in the city.
“If Persuasion’s grace be sacred to thee ... Tarry, I pray thee.” They stay, as the city's kindly guardians.
You are Oedipus, prince of Corinth. At Delphi the god told you: you will kill your father and marry your mother.
So you will never go home to Corinth, to the king and queen you love. You take the road the other way.

steps.text: Walk on to where three roads meet

steps.line: “A herald met me and a man who sat In a car drawn by colts ... Threatened to thrust me rudely from the path.”
“The old man ... from his car brought down Full on my head the double-pointed goad.”
“One stroke Of my good staff sufficed to fling him clean Out of the chariot seat ... And so I slew them every one.”
You never asked his name. He was Laius, King of Thebes. You walk on to Thebes, and the Sphinx, and the queen.
The plague is still killing Thebes. A messenger from Corinth says: the king you called your father was not your father.
“Know that he took thee from my hands, a gift.” He had you as a baby from a Theban shepherd, your ankles pinned.
Jocasta begs you to stop asking. She has understood. She goes into the house.

steps.text: Stand before the altar, where the old shepherd waits

steps.act: Make him tell you, and do not stop

steps.line: The child he was given to kill was Laius's, and Jocasta's. He could not do it. He gave it away. It was you.
“Ah me! ah me! all brought to pass, all true! O light, may I behold thee nevermore!”

steps.text: Go into the house

steps.line: He found her hanged. “He tore the golden brooches that upheld Her queenly robes, upraised them high and smote.”
“Therefore wait to see life’s ending ere thou count one mortal blest.”
You are Antigone, daughter of Oedipus. Your brothers killed each other at the gates, one defending Thebes, one attacking it.
King Creon has ordered: Polynices, the traitor, lies unburied for the dogs and birds. Whoever buries him dies.

steps.text: Go out to your brother's body

steps.act: Sprinkle dust over him, and pour the offerings

steps.line: “The corpse is buried; someone E’en now besprinkled it with thirsty dust.” The guards take you to the king.
“The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven. They were not born today nor yesterday; They die not.”
“My nature is for mutual love, not hate.” “Die then, and love the dead if thou must.”

steps.text: Walk into the tomb

steps.line: He walls you up alive. Teiresias warns him; he gives way at last, and comes to open the tomb. Too late.
You are Pentheus, king of Thebes. You come home to find the women gone to the mountain, and your old grandfather in a fawnskin.
“Track out this effeminate stranger, who brings this new disease upon women, and pollutes our beds.”

steps.act: Have him bound and shut in the stables

steps.line: He goes quietly, smiling. “Finding a bull in the stable ... he cast halters round the knees of that.”
The ground shakes. Fire leaps from Semele's tomb, and your palace cracks. The stranger walks out, free, unhurried.
“I would rather sacrifice to him than, being wrath, kick against the pricks; a mortal against a God.”
“I will sacrifice, making a great slaughter of the women, as they deserve, in the glens of Cithæron.”
“Do you no longer wish to be a spectator of the Mænads?” You do. More than anything.
“With what dress—a woman’s? but shame possesses me.” “I will spread out your hair at length on your head.”

steps.act: Put on the long linen dress

steps.line: “And indeed I think I see two suns, and twin Thebes, and seven-gated city.”
“You seem to guide me, being like a bull, and horns seem to grow on your head.”

steps.text: Follow the stranger toward the mountain

steps.line: “You alone labor for this city, you alone; therefore the labors, which are meet, await you.”

steps.text: Creep down toward the glade

steps.line: The stranger takes the top of a tall fir, “pulled it down, pulled it, pulled it to the dark earth, and it was bent like a bow.”
“Having placed Pentheus on the pine branches, he let it go upright through his hands steadily.”
A voice from the sky: here is the man who mocks you. The women see him. His mother is the first to reach the tree.
“I have caught him without a noose, a young lion, as you may see.” Agave comes down the mountain rejoicing.
Her father Cadmus makes her look, slowly, at what she carries. It is her son's head.
“Ye have learned it too late; but when it behooved you, you knew it not.”
“Ah me! Ah me! O King Jupiter, of what a terrible length the nights are! Will it never be day?”
“I am not able, miserable man, to sleep, being tormented by my expenses, and my stud of horses, and my debts.”

steps.act: Light the lamp and count your debts

steps.line: “What do I owe? Twelve minæ to Pasias. Why twelve minæ to Pasias? ... When I bought the blood-horse. Ah me!”
Your son, asleep in five blankets, dreams of the races: “You are acting unfairly, Philo! Drive on your own course.”
“Do you see this little door and little house? ... This is a thinking-shop of wise spirits.”
They teach, you hear, the worse argument, the one that wins though it speaks on the unjust side. No more debts.

steps.text: Go to the Thinkery's door

steps.line: A pupil tells you the mysteries: Socrates lately worked out how many of its own feet a flea can jump.
“Socrates! My little Socrates!” “Why callest thou me, thou creature of a day?”
“I am walking in the air, and speculating about the sun.”
“Who is it that compels them to borne along? Is it not Jupiter?” “By no means, but æthereal Vortex.”

steps.act: Sit on the sacred couch, and meet the Clouds

steps.line: “Will you not, pray, now believe in no god, except what we believe in—this Chaos, and the Clouds, and the Tongue?”
Your son has beaten you, and proved it just. The Clouds tell you: this is what comes of loving what is wicked.
“Come forth with a ladder and with a mattock and then mount upon the thinking-shop and dig down the roof.”

steps.text: Set up the ladder

steps.act: Tear at the roof with the mattock

steps.line: The pupils run out coughing. Socrates chokes in the smoke. The audience laughs; the play is over.
In 399 BC, on trial for his life, Socrates told the jurors his oldest accusers were not his prosecutors, but this play.
